title: SRE runtime contracts and capacity safety-net patterns
author: Maya Chen
body:
Overview

This page defines a lightweight, repeatable "service resilience contract" that binds SLOs to concrete capacity safety-nets and runtime degradation behaviors. The goal is to give product and SRE teams a shared, actionable agreement for how an application will behave as it consumes its error budget, and which capacity operations are authorized at each step.

Purpose

- Establish explicit mappings from SLO thresholds and error-budget burn rates to capacity/autoscale actions, rollout safeguards, and graceful-degradation policies.
- Reduce decision latency during incidents by pre-authorizing safe mitigations.
- Standardize telemetry and runbook playbooks so service owners can validate readiness in advance.

Scope

Applies to services owned by Platform, Serving, and Product teams that expose public inference endpoints (hosted, dedicated, or private). This includes model-serving frontends, inference routers, and orchestration proxies integrated with the Redwood runtime. Does not replace service-specific runbooks for data-plane bugs, but augments them with SLO-linked capacity actions.

Service resilience contract template (fill per service)

Title: <service-name> resilience contract
Service owner: <team>
Primary contact: <oncall alias>
SLO(s):
- Availability SLO: 99.9% p99 over 30d (or other agreed window)
- Latency SLO: p95 latency < 1200ms for text generation endpoints
Error budget allocation: monthly, with burn alert at 10% remaining (see alarms)
Capacity safety-net tiers (authorized actions):
1) Tier A (conservative): automated burst autoscale up to +25% baseline GPU pool; no model swaps; require Ops review for scaling beyond.
2) Tier B (aggressive): scale to reserved spare pool / cross-region failover with automatic model-variant fallback (quantized model) enabled.
3) Tier C (degrade): enable structured degradation (synthetic throttling / reduced beam width / cache-only mode) and route remaining requests to a low-cost model variant.

Degradation matrix (use as decision table)

| Condition | Error-budget remaining | Immediate action | Authorization | Expected RTO |
|---|---:|---|---|---:|
| Normal | > 50% | No action | N/A | N/A |
| Elevated | 20% - 50% | Enable Tier A burst autoscale; increase request sampling to 5% | Service owner | 5–15m |
| At risk | 10% - 20% | Prepare Tier B; warm reserved pool; enable model-variant fallback (quantized) | SRE + Service owner | 10–30m |
| Critical | <= 10% | Apply Tier C graceful degradation; circuit to cache-only routing; restrict heavy pipelines | SRE escalation | 1–15m |

Notes:
- "Authorization" defines who can trigger the action without exec-committee approval. SRE oncall may act within Tier A and Tier C and must notify owners; Tier B requires explicit owner sign-off unless automated pre-authorized in the contract.

Operational runbooks: step-by-step

1) Detection and validation (oncall)
   - Check the primary SLO alerting dashboard and error-budget burn rate.
   - Verify traffic pattern change with request-rate (RPS) and p95/p99 latency graphs.
   - If burn rate > 2x expected baseline and error budget <= 20%, escalate to oncall lead.

2) Activate Tier A (automated)
   - Command: ./infractl scale --service <service-name> --pool burst --delta 25%
   - Validate: successful pool resize events in infra-events stream and <service>-pool-utilization < 85%.
   - Observe for 10 minutes. If improvement in p95 latency > 10% and error budget burn drops, continue to monitor.

3) Prepare Tier B (authorization required if not pre-authorized)
   - Warm reserved pool: /infra/warm-pool --pool reserved-<region> --size 1-2-nodes
   - Toggle model fallback: POST /api/rollouts/<service>/activate-variant {"variant":"quantized-v1"}
   - Validate: KV cache population and model warm-start logs show baseline latencies.

4) Enact Tier C (immediate for critical)
   - Enable cache-only routing: /gateway/route --service <service> --policy cache-first
   - Apply request-level soft-throttle: rate-limit by token-budget header at 70%
   - Reduce sample sizes or disable expensive reranking or long-context pipelines.

5) Recovery and rollback
   - Observe error-budget burn rates returning to baseline for 2 full monitoring windows (default 30m windows).
   - Rollback steps reverse the actions in the inverse order used to escalate: remove tier-C throttles, disable fallback model, scale down burst pool.
   - Document incident summary and update the resilience contract if actions were insufficient.

Telemetry, alerts, and dashboards

Required telemetry per service:
- SLO-burn-rate (1m, 5m, 30m) — primary composite metric
- p95 and p99 latency per route/model variant
- request RPS, request size histogram, token-per-request distribution
- pool utilization per GPU pool and per-region allocation
- cold-start count and model load durations

Prometheus examples (PromQL):
- SLO burn rate (error count / error budget): sum(rate(request_errors_total[5m])) / oncall:avg_error_budget
- p95 latency: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_latency_bucket[5m])) by (le))

Key alerts and thresholds:
- slo_burn_rate_5m > 1.5 for 15m -> P2 alert to oncall
- slo_remaining <= 10% -> P1 urgent page to SRE and product owner
- pool_utilization_gpu > 90% for 10m -> P2 to infra and oncall

Policy for autoscale and reserved capacity

Autoscale guardrails (always enforced):
- Max burst autoscale delta: 40% of baseline without business-owner sign-off.
- Autoscale cooldown: 5m min, 20m max depending on observed tail latency.
- Pre-warmed reserved pool must achieve > 70% of model warm-start readiness before routing critical traffic.

Reserved capacity and economic fallback

- Services with SLO > 99.9% must maintain a minimum reserved capacity equivalent to 15% of 95th-percentile sustained demand.
- For cost-aware services (internal or dev tiers), pre-authorized fallback model variants (quantized or distilled) must be trained to match safety, privacy, and semantic fidelity minimums, and included in the contract with validation metrics.

Incident postmortem & contract update procedure

1) Within 48 hours: preliminary incident timeline added to the incident review doc and a blameless hypothesis documented.
2) Within 7 days: full post-incident review with telemetry, root-cause hypotheses, and a list of proposed contract changes.
3) Contract revision: if a safety-net action activated more than once in the previous 90 days, the contract must be updated to specify additional pre-authorized capacity or a longer-term mitigation.

Ownership and responsibilities

- Service owner: defines SLO targets, approves Tier B default behaviors, and participates in post-incident updates.
- SRE oncall: authorized to operate Tier A and Tier C actions, to coordinate cross-team scaling, and to raise Tier B approval requests.
- Infra team: owns reserved pool management and warm-pool APIs.
- Observability: maintains SLO dashboards, alerting rules, and related runbook documentation.

Appendix: example configuration snippets

YAML guardrail example (for infra pipeline):

---
service: inference-frontend
autoscale:
  baseline_replicas: 10
  max_burst_percent: 40  # enforced guardrail
  cooldown_policy:
    min: 300  # seconds
    max: 1200
reserved_capacity:
  required_percent_of_95th: 15
  warm_pool_size: 2

Example infractl commands
- ./infractl scale --service inference-frontend --pool burst --delta 25%
- ./infractl warm --pool reserved-us-west-2 --service inference-frontend --nodes 2
- curl -X POST "https://console.internal/api/rollouts/inference-frontend/activate-variant" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"variant":"quantized-v2"}'

Example PromQL snippets (copy/paste)
- p95 latency: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(inference_request_latency_bucket[5m])) by (le,service))
- slo remaining (30d window): (720 - sum(increase(service_errors_total[30d]))) / 720  # if 720 allowed errors per window

Review cadence and lifecycle

- Contracts must be reviewed quarterly by the service owner and SRE lead.
- If a service changes model architecture or adds a heavy pipeline (e.g., reranker, multi-pass generation), the contract must be revalidated before the change reaches prod.
